meta.title: Who really said "Carpe diem"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: "Carpe diem" is genuinely Horace's — it closes his Odes 1.11 (23 BC). But it literally means "pluck the day," and the two words are only half his actual line.
meta.ogDescription: Yes, it's Horace — Odes 1.11, 23 BC. But he wrote "pluck," not "seize," and the famous two words are only half of a longer sentence.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The two words “carpe diem” are Horace’s own Latin, closing his Odes 1.11 (published 23 BC): “carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero.” This is verified against the Latin text — but note the popular gloss “seize the day” sharpens Horace’s horticultural metaphor, which is closer to “pluck the day.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero” (the closing line)
Original Latin — not an English translation

source.excerpt: Dum loquimur, fugerit invida aetas: carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero. — “While we speak, envious time will have fled: pluck the day, trusting as little as possible in the next one.”
trail: The phrase closes Horace’s Odes 1.11 ↗, part of Book 1 of the Odes, published 23 BC.
The Latin line — “carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero” — is preserved in the Perseus edition of the Latin text ↗.
Carpe is a horticultural verb, “pick / pluck”; the more literal reading is “pluck the day ↗,” not the more forceful popular “seize the day.”
source.excerptNote: The famous tag is only the first two words of a longer clause; Horace’s full thought couples enjoying the present with distrust of the future.

source.rightsNote: The displayed wording is Horace’s original Latin, written in 23 BC — ancient text in the public domain. (Any specific modern English translation, such as “seize the day,” may carry its own copyright, but the Latin tag itself does not.)

author.metaLine: 65 BC – 8 BC · Roman lyric poet of the Augustan age
author.bio: Quintus Horatius Flaccus, known as Horace, was the leading Roman lyric poet under the emperor Augustus. His four books of Odes (Carmina) reworked Greek lyric metres into Latin and gave the language enduring tags such as carpe diem and nunc est bibendum. Ode 1.11, addressed to a woman named Leuconoe, urges her to stop reading horoscopes and enjoy the fleeting present.

misattribution.heading: The catch isn't who — it's what it means
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is solid: “carpe diem” really is Horace’s Latin. The distortion is in the meaning and in quoting only half the line.

items.why: Carpe is a gardening word — to pick or pluck ripe fruit. The forceful English “seize” overstates it; scholars note the more literal “pluck the day ↗” better fits Horace’s image of savouring the moment as it ripens.

“Carpe diem” is usually quoted alone, but Horace wrote “carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero” — “…trusting as little as possible in tomorrow ↗.” The clipped version reads as pure hedonism; the full line is really about the uncertainty of the future.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are genuinely Horace’s, from Odes 1.11 ↗ — but he wrote “pluck,” not “seize,” and only ever as the first half of a longer, more cautious thought.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Horace published his first three books of Odes in 23 BC, adapting the metres and moods of Greek lyric poets like Alcaeus and Sappho into Latin. Ode 1.11 is a short poem to a woman called Leuconoe, warning her against Babylonian astrology and the wish to know how long she has to live.

The two-word phrase became a cultural motto far larger than the poem — a banner for everything from Renaissance verse to Dead Poets Society. Its afterlife often flattens Horace’s point: not reckless indulgence, but a measured, almost Epicurean acceptance that the future is unknowable, so the ripe present should not be wasted.
context.pull: “Pluck the day, trusting as little as possible in the next one.”
